units.name: Everyday life, money and how we describe it

lessons.title: Heartbreak and rough patches
lessons.goal: By the end you can talk about a difficult time in a relationship or friendship: what happened, when it happened and how long it lasted.

sources.title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Today we talk about love, friendship and the hard times in between. First you answer a few questions about yourself and meet the key phrases. Then you listen to two presenters discuss why a broken heart really hurts, and you test how much you caught. These are the words you need when a friend asks, 'So, how are things with you two?'
steps.ru: Сегодня говорим об отношениях, дружбе и трудных периодах. Сначала отвечаете на вопросы о себе и знакомитесь с фразами, потом слушаете, почему разбитое сердце болит по-настоящему, и проверяете, что поняли.

steps.title: Warm up
qs: Think of a friendship or relationship of yours that went through a bumpy time. What was going on, and what finally got you through it?
When you feel low, what do the people around you usually do to cheer you up? Does it work, or would you rather be left alone?
Think back to the last time you fell out with someone close. Who made the first move to make up, and how did it happen?
Do you think falling in love is something you choose or something that simply happens to you? And is there anything in your daily life that you are a little bit addicted to?
steps.hint: Type one to three sentences for each question; there are no wrong answers, just say what you really think.

items.ex: We went through a rough patch last year, but we talked it out and things are much better now.
I fell in love with Lisbon the minute I stepped off the plane.
He had his heart broken at nineteen, and he still doesn't like to talk about it.
When I think back to my first job, I can't believe how nervous I was.
I bought her a cake to cheer her up after the exam.
I've been feeling a bit down since the clocks changed, to be honest.
We had a stupid argument on Friday, but we made up before the weekend.
I'll ring my sister for a chat on the way home; I haven't spoken to her all week.
I'm completely addicted to this series; I watched four episodes last night.
Funnily enough, I'm still good friends with my ex.

items.ru: пережить трудное время и выбраться из него
items.ex: It was a tough year, but we came out the other side stronger.
In a long relationship, it's all about listening to each other.

qs.q: Complete the dialogue. 'How are things with Dan?' 'Not brilliant. We're ___ at the moment, but I think we'll sort it out.'
o: going through a rough patch
making up a rough patch
thinking back to a rough patch
cheering up a rough patch
qs.why: 'Go through a rough patch' means to have a difficult but temporary period; the other verbs do not combine with 'rough patch' in this way.

qs.q: Mira texted first after a week of silence, and by the evening they had made up. What does 'made up' mean here?
o: stopped being angry and became friends again
invented a story to explain the argument
agreed to meet again at some later date
decided to end the friendship politely
qs.why: 'Make up' as a phrasal verb about people means to end a quarrel and be friends again.

qs.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: A silly video cheered me up straight away.
A silly video cheered up me straight away.
A silly video cheered me down straight away.
A silly video made me to cheer up straight away.
qs.why: When the object is a pronoun, it goes in the middle: cheer me up, cheer him up.

qs.q: 'When I think back to our first year in Glasgow, we had no money but we laughed all the time.' Here, 'think back to' means:
o: remember a past period and reflect on it
plan carefully for a coming period
feel sorry about a past decision
return to a place you lived in before
qs.why: 'Think back to' is about calling a past time to mind in your head, not about going anywhere.

qs.q: 'Was the divorce hard on her?' 'Brutal for about two years. But she's ___ now and has started her own business.'
o: come out the other side
come over the other side
gone out from the other side
got off the other side
qs.why: 'Come out the other side' is the fixed phrase for surviving a hard time and being fine afterwards.

qs.q: 'In a friendship, it's all about trust.' What does 'it's all about' mean here?
o: trust is the thing that matters most
trust is what people talk about most
trust is the first thing that you lose
trust is something to be proud of
qs.why: 'It's all about X' says that X is the most important point or the real secret.

qs.q: Which sentence is NOT close in meaning to 'I'm addicted to this series'?
o: I'm fed up with this series.
I'm hooked on this series.
I can't stop watching this series.
I need my next episode every night.
qs.why: 'Addicted to' means you want more all the time; being fed up is the opposite feeling.

qs.q: 'He had his heart broken at nineteen.' What does this tell us?
o: Someone he loved hurt him badly, probably by leaving
He had a serious heart operation as a teenager
He broke a girlfriend's heart by leaving her
He lost all of his savings when he was nineteen
qs.why: 'Have your heart broken' means you were the one hurt; if you did the hurting, you 'broke someone's heart'.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: Listen once without the text and keep three gist questions in mind: What happens in the brain when we fall in love? Why did our brains evolve like this, and is it good for us? What happens in the brain after a break-up? Then read the transcript, underline the phrases from your list and notice how Neil and Georgie sound natural. Do not look up every word.

qs.q: Which order do the main ideas come in?
o: Scans of people in love, the survival idea, the 2013 study, social bonds and health, scans of exes
Scans of exes, the survival idea, scans of people in love, the 2013 study, social bonds and health
Social bonds and health, scans of people in love, the survival idea, scans of exes, the 2013 study
The 2013 study, scans of people in love, the survival idea, scans of exes, social bonds and health
qs.why: The presenters move from love scans to survival, then the identity study, then the health benefits of bonds, and only at the end to heartbreak and exes.

qs.q: Neil says the part of the brain used for thinking about ourselves 'lit up'. Here, 'lit up' means that it:
o: became active and showed up on the scan
stopped working for a few seconds
became larger in the volunteers
felt painful to the volunteers
qs.why: On a brain scan, an area that 'lights up' is one that is active; Zoe Donaldson uses the same idea for pain regions.

qs.q: Who explains that 'addicted' can be used about things we love, not only about drugs or alcohol?
o: Georgie
Neil
Dr Lucy Brown
Professor Zoe Donaldson
qs.why: After Lucy's clip, Georgie says we use 'addicted' metaphorically for things we love; Neil then explains 'orientated'.

qs.q: Why does Neil say that being in love changes 'our whole identity'?
o: Statements about a partner lit up the same area as statements about oneself.
Statements about a partner lit up the area used for thinking about other people.
Statements about oneself no longer lit up any area once people fell in love.
People in love described themselves using the words they used for their partners.
qs.why: In the 2013 study the partner statements activated the 'self' area, not the area we usually use for other people.

qs.q: What does Dr Lucy Brown mean by calling love 'a survival system'?
o: Nature gave us the urge to bond because it helps us reproduce and stay protected.
People learn to bond only after they have survived a painful break-up.
Being in love replaces hunger and thirst, so people can live on less food.
Lonely people develop special brain systems that help them to survive alone.
qs.why: She says nature gave us these systems for reproduction and protection, and compares the feeling to hunger or thirst.

qs.q: Which conclusion fits what Zoe Donaldson says about loneliness?
o: Having no close bonds can endanger health as seriously as smoking does.
Obese people and smokers are usually lonelier than other people.
Lonely people are certain to die earlier than people with friends.
Loneliness is dangerous mainly for people who already suffer from depression.
qs.why: She says the mortality risk of being lonely goes up in a way that is equivalent to being obese or smoking; she does not say it is certain or limited to depression.

qs.q: Zoe Donaldson says the brain regions for heartbreak 'overlap' with those for physical pain. She means that:
o: they partly share the same regions
one is felt more strongly than the other
they use regions that are far apart
one always appears before the other
qs.why: 'Overlap' means partly the same; she says the lit-up areas coincide with those active when you get a burn or break a bone.

qs.q: As Lucy Brown uses it, being 'oriented toward the other person' means that:
o: that person is your main focus and comes first in your thoughts
you gradually start copying that person's habits
you physically turn to face them whenever they speak
you feel responsible for that person's safety
qs.why: Neil explains it as thinking of each other before other people; it is a metaphor, not a physical position.

qs.q: Zoe calls strong social bonds 'the number one predictor of longevity'. In this sentence, a 'predictor' is:
o: a factor that helps you forecast how long people will live
a doctor who studies how long people live
a medicine that makes people live longer
a rule that sets the age at which people die
qs.why: Neil defines longevity as how long we live, so a predictor of it is something that tells you how likely a long life is.

qs.q: When did Georgie say her heart was last broken, and when did psychologists notice the link in the quiz question?
o: A couple of years ago; in the 1950s
About ten years ago; in the 1950s
A couple of years ago; in the 1990s
Last winter; in 2013
qs.why: Georgie says it was a couple of years ago, and the quiz question places attachment theory in the 1950s.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.prompt: Write 6 to 8 sentences about a difficult time in a friendship or relationship, yours or someone else's. Say what happened, how long it lasted and how you or they felt. Use at least six phrases from today's list, and include at least one 'for' or 'since' expression to show how long.
steps.hint: Start with 'A few years ago, a close friend of mine went through a rough patch...'.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: In Part 2 we warm up, check what you remember, and listen to a short episode about one very useful expression. Then we go deeper into the tenses we need to talk about a relationship over time, including the ones that tell the reader how long something had lasted, and you finish by telling your own story out loud.
steps.ru: Во второй части: разминка, повторение фраз, короткий эпизод про одно полезное выражение, более глубокий разбор времён для рассказа об отношениях и их длительности и, наконец, ваш собственный рассказ вслух.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: Listen first without the text and notice the three situations that the speakers use as examples of the expression. Then read the transcript, underline every use of it and note the two other words that can replace 'rough'.

steps.title: Grammar: perfect tenses and narrative
steps.text: Choose by time frame and by focus. The past simple closes a story in a finished period ('We split up in March'), while the present perfect keeps the period open or cares about the result now ('We've split up, so please don't ask'). The continuous form puts the spotlight on the activity or its duration, even if it has just stopped ('You've been crying'); the simple form puts it on the result or the number ('I've written three apologies'), and state verbs such as know or be stay simple. In a story, use the past simple for main events, the past continuous for the background, the past perfect for what came earlier, and the past perfect continuous for how long something had been going on before a past moment.
steps.ru: Выбор зависит от рамки времени и акцента. Past simple: закончившийся период, событие в прошлом. Present perfect: период не закончен или важен результат сейчас. Continuous подчёркивает процесс и длительность (даже если он только что закончился), simple подчёркивает результат и количество; глаголы состояния (know, be) остаются в simple. В рассказе: past simple для главных событий, past continuous для фона, past perfect для того, что было раньше, past perfect continuous для длительности до момента в прошлом.
ex: We split up in March, but I've only just stopped checking his profile.
You look shattered. Have you been arguing again?
She has sent him four messages today and has been waiting for an answer since lunchtime.
It's the third time they've gone through a rough patch, and it's ages since they last had a proper holiday.
By the time he rang her, she had been waiting for weeks, and she had already decided to move on.
I was queuing for coffee when my ex called. We hadn't spoken since we split up, and I had been dreading that call for months.

items.s: Your eyes are red. ___ (you / cry)?
She ___ (send) him four messages today, and he hasn't answered any of them.
items.hint: present perfect simple, number of times

items.s: We ___ (be) close friends ever since we shared a desk at primary school.
Have you seen Ana? - Yes, I ___ (see) her at the station an hour ago.
She told me she ___ (look) for a flat since October, which is why she looked so tired.
I ___ (walk) home when my ex called, and I almost dropped my phone.
How long ___ (it / be) since you last spoke to her?
This is the first time we ___ (argue) in front of the children.
No sooner ___ we made up than we started arguing about money again.
By next June, we ___ (be) together for ten years.
I regret not telling her the truth. -> I wish I ___ her the truth.
Kat ___ (go) through a rough patch for months now, so be gentle with her.

steps.title: Say it
steps.prompt: Tell the story of a friendship or relationship, yours or a friend's: how it began, what was going on in the background, what went wrong before things changed, and how long it has lasted since. Try to use at least three different tenses from the grammar step.
steps.model: My friend Dasha and I have been friends since university. We were sharing a flat when everything went wrong. By the time she finally told me she was upset, I had been ignoring her messages for weeks, because I was feeling down about my job. Honestly, it was my fault. We went through a rough patch for about three months, and then she rang me for a chat out of the blue. We made up in ten minutes. Looking back, it's all about being honest with each other. We came out the other side, and we've been closer ever since.

lessons.title: Asking and saying no
lessons.goal: By the end you can make a request without sounding pushy, turn one down politely, report what was said with precise verbs, and talk about how it feels to be rejected.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Most of us find it harder to ask for something than to answer a question, and harder still to hear 'no'. First you will think about your own experience and meet twelve phrases. Then you will listen to a BBC programme about people who walk up to strangers and ask for odd things, answer ten careful questions about it, and write a short text of your own.
steps.ru: Просить и слышать отказ на живом английском непросто. Сначала подумаем о себе и разберём 12 фраз, потом послушаем передачу BBC про людей, которые просят о странном незнакомцев, ответим на 10 вопросов и напишем свой текст.

steps.title: Warm up
qs: When did you last ask somebody for a favour that felt a little awkward? What made it hard to ask, and what did you say in the end?
Think of something that frightened you the first time you did it, but got easier with practice. What was it, and when did you stop worrying?
Which do you find harder: asking for help or saying no to people? Where do you think that comes from?
Is being turned down always a bad thing? Describe a time when a no turned out to be good for you, or at least taught you something.
steps.hint: Answer each question in one to three sentences. There are no right answers: say what is true for you.

items.ru: непростая просьба, требование (то, о чём трудно просить)
items.ex: Moving the whole launch forward by a week is a big ask, to be honest.
Can I ask you a favour? Would you water my plants while I'm away?
I never thought I'd enjoy early mornings, but you get used to them.
I'd never cooked fish before, but I had a go at it last night.

items.ru: узнать, как у кого-то всё прошло
items.ex: Let's ring Anna later and see how she got on at the interview.
I hate heights, so climbing that tower was my way of facing my fears.
Speaking up in meetings was scary at first, but it comes easier every time.

items.ru: мне было интересно, не могли бы вы... (мягкая просьба)
items.ex: I was wondering if you could look at my presentation before Friday.
Can I try this chair out before I decide whether to buy it?
A few kind words from a good teacher can boost your confidence for weeks.
You're busy tonight? No problem, I get it.
Sorry, I mixed up the dates and turned up a day early.

qs.q: Complete the reply. 'Could you look after my dog for the whole of August?' 'Hmm, that is quite ___, to be honest.'
o: a big ask
a close call
a fair swap
a nice try
qs.why: A big ask is a request that you know will be difficult for the other person.

qs.q: After a month in Dublin, Marta has finally got used to the rain. What does this mean?
o: The rain no longer feels strange or annoying to her.
She has learnt how to stay dry whatever the weather.
She has started to enjoy rain more than sunshine.
She has decided to move away because of the weather.
qs.why: To get used to something is to stop finding it strange or difficult.

qs.q: Which sentence uses 'have a go at' correctly?
o: I've never tried pottery, so I'd love to have a go at it.
I had a go at the station and then caught the train home.
She has a go at a quarter past nine every single day.
We had a go at the weekend in the mountains last year.
qs.why: To have a go at something is to try it, usually for the first time.

qs.q: Dan had his job interview this morning. I'll text him tonight to see how he ___.
o: got on
got over
got up
got off
qs.why: See how someone got on means find out how things went for them.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT a way of saying that you 'try out' a new gym?
o: walk past it without ever going inside
test it for a week before paying
give it a go for a couple of sessions
see what it is like by visiting it once
qs.why: Trying something out means actually using it to see what it is like; walking past is the opposite.

qs.q: 'It was hard at first, but it came easier.' What does this mean?
o: It became less difficult as I kept doing it.
It arrived earlier than I had planned.
Someone else began to do it for me.
I decided that it was not worth doing.
qs.why: If something comes easier, it becomes easier to achieve, usually through practice.

qs.q: Which request sounds the most tentative and polite?
o: I was wondering if you might be able to help me move on Sunday.
Can you help me move flat on Sunday, please?
You are going to help me move flat on Sunday.
Will you help me move flat on Sunday, then?
qs.why: The continuous past plus 'if' and 'might' puts the most distance between speaker and request.

qs.q: Complete the apology. 'I'm sorry, I'm a day early: I ___ the dates and thought the meeting was today.'
o: mixed up
mixed in
mixed out
mixed off
qs.why: Mix up the dates means to confuse them, so you get the wrong day.

o: It is an online trend that has not been tested.
Doctors now prescribe it for shy patients.
It was created by the BBC World Service.

qs.q: What is Neil's own view of experiencing rejection?

It should be avoided because it damages confidence.

qs.q: How did Georgie's guess about Walt Disney turn out?
o: She was wrong: the claim that did not happen was about his first film.
She was right: the claim that did not happen was about his job.
She was wrong: the claim that did not happen was about his business.
She made no guess because she already knew the answer.

qs.q: Which of Hannah's requests did she not expect to be accepted?

Sitting down at a stranger's table
Asking someone how their day had gone
Greeting a person in the afternoon

qs.q: By which attempt did Hannah no longer mind whether the answer was yes or no?
o: The fourth
The second
The third
The tenth

qs.q: What does Claudia Hammond say she actually KNOWS, as opposed to merely wonders about?
o: That perfectionism is on the rise
That the videos improve people's confidence
That young people now avoid talking to strangers
That filming strangers upsets most of them
qs.why: She says 'what we do know' is that perfectionism is increasing; the link to shyness she only wonders about.

qs.q: Hannah says she 'didn't even mind it' by the fourth time. Here 'mind' means ___.
o: feel bothered by it
keep it in her memory
take care of it
look forward to it

qs.q: Claudia says young people worry that others will not 'appraise them in a good way'. Here 'appraise' means ___.
o: form a judgement of them
give them a reward
record them on video
copy their behaviour
qs.why: The presenters explain it in the vocabulary recap: to appraise someone is to judge them.

qs.q: Claudia suggests the videos might 'counter' perfectionist worries. Here 'counter' means ___.
o: work against them
make them worse
count them up
agree with them

qs.q: What does Hannah's experiment seem to suggest about asking strangers for things?
o: People are often kinder than we fear.
Most people refuse unless you pay them.
Cab drivers are the least friendly people.

steps.how: Listen once without the text with two questions in mind: what exactly does Phil ask for, and how does Feifei say no without being rude? Then read the transcript and underline the polite phrases. Notice how Phil softens his request before he makes it.

steps.title: Grammar: distance in requests, refusals and reports
steps.text: At C1, politeness is mostly about distance. A past or continuous form pushes a request away from the listener, so 'I was hoping you might...' and 'I was wondering if you could...' sound softer than 'Can you...?', and 'I don't suppose you could..., could you?' or 'Would you mind if I opened the window?' soften it further. In an indirect question the clause after the opener keeps statement order and takes if or whether ('Do you happen to know whether she has left?'), but after 'do you think' the question word moves to the front ('Where do you think she has gone?'). To refuse, soften the verb and give a reason: 'I'm afraid I won't be able to', 'I'd rather not, if you don't mind', 'Much as I'd like to, I can't'. When you report such a moment, choose a verb that shows what the person did and mind its pattern: refuse + to-infinitive, admit + -ing, insist on + -ing, suggest + (that) I ask.
steps.ru: Вежливость в английском строится на дистанции: прошедшее и длительное время (I was hoping, I was wondering) смягчают просьбу. В косвенном вопросе порядок слов прямой, с if/whether, но после do you think вопросительное слово идёт вперёд. Отказ смягчают так: I'm afraid I won't be able to, I'd rather not, Much as I'd like to. В пересказе выбирай точный глагол и его модель: refuse to, admit -ing, insist on, suggest (that) I ask.
ex: I was hoping you might be able to cover my shift on Friday.
I don't suppose you'd mind swapping seats, would you?
Do you happen to know whether the office is open on Sundays?
Why do you think he turned us down so quickly?
Much as I'd like to help, I'm afraid I won't be able to make it on Saturday.
He admitted mixing up the dates, but refused to change his plans, and she suggested that he ask someone else.

Could you tell me ___ the pharmacy is open on Sundays?

steps.title: Say it
steps.prompt: Tell the story of a time you made a difficult request or had to turn one down. Say what you asked or were asked, how it was worded, what the other person said, and how you both felt afterwards. Try to use a softened request, an indirect question, a polite refusal and at least one precise reporting verb such as refuse, admit or suggest.
steps.model: Last spring a colleague asked me to cover her whole weekend shift. Much as I'd like to have helped, I was already booked, so I told her it was a big ask and said no. Then I added, 'I was wondering if Tom might be free instead? I don't suppose you've asked him yet, have you?' She admitted she hadn't, and she laughed and said, 'OK, I get it.' I used to find saying no really awkward, but it has come easier since then. In the end Tom agreed without any fuss.

lessons.title: Reading between the lines
lessons.goal: By the end you can soften what you say, make careful guesses about what people really meant (must have, might have, can't have, seems to have), and answer an unexpected question without freezing.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: British people often say one thing and mean another. Today you will first think about your own habits, then meet twelve useful phrases, then hear two presenters explain how exaggeration, understatement and polite little phrases work. It is the last lesson of Unit 1, so everything you have practised so far (feelings, asking, refusing) comes together.
steps.ru: Британцы часто говорят одно, а имеют в виду другое. Сначала вы подумаете о себе, потом познакомитесь с фразами, а затем послушаете, как это работает, и научитесь читать между строк.

steps.title: Warm up
qs: Think of the last time you had to answer a question or make a decision with no time to prepare. What happened, and how did you cope?
Is there something that is simply not acceptable in your family, your school or your workplace, even though nobody ever wrote it down? How would a newcomer find out?
When someone says 'no problem' but you suspect they are slightly annoyed, what usually gives them away: their words, their face, or something else?
When you tell a friend about a bad day, do you tend to make it sound worse than it was, or better? Describe your last difficult day the way you would really tell it.
steps.hint: Answer in one to three sentences each. Do not worry about perfect English: you will meet useful phrases for these answers in a moment.

items.ex: When the interviewer changed the question, Anna had to think on her feet.

items.ru: сообразить прямо на месте, без подготовки
items.ex: She asked me for a new slogan and I had to think on the spot.
He is great fun because he never takes himself too seriously.
In my office it's not the done thing to send emails after nine at night.
Checking your phone during dinner is a total no-no in our family.
I was a bit miffed that nobody had asked for my opinion.
I didn't want to get into a barney over who had forgotten the tickets.

items.ru: всё нормально (а на деле, возможно, не очень)
items.ex: She said it's all good when I turned up late, but her face said something else.
Sorry I'm late! - No worries, we've only just started.
I've had a mare of a morning: the bus never came and my phone died.
Let's not get into a whole thing about it tonight.
The hotel was, let's say, less than perfect: there was no hot water for two days.

qs.q: Complete the dialogue. 'Sorry, I've kept you waiting for ages!' - '___, I only got here myself five minutes ago.'
o: No worries
It's a no-no
It's the done thing
I'm having a mare
qs.why: No worries is the casual way of saying that there is no problem.

qs.q: 'The projector died ten seconds before his talk, so he had to think on his feet.' What did he have to do?
o: Improvise a solution quickly under pressure
Stand up and walk around to stay calm
Ask the audience to decide for him
Cancel the talk and start again later
qs.why: Think on your feet means to think and decide quickly when there is no time to prepare.

qs.q: 'Dan looked rather miffed when his idea was ignored.' How did Dan feel?
o: Slightly annoyed and put out
Deeply hurt and close to tears
Quietly relieved and calm
Totally lost and confused
qs.why: Miffed is a mild word: slightly annoyed by someone's behaviour.

qs.q: Which sentence uses 'the done thing' correctly?
o: In many families it's the done thing to bring a small gift when you visit.
The lift is broken again, which is really not the done thing.
He did the done thing and wrote the whole report in one night.
It's the done thing to feel tired after a long flight, isn't it?
qs.why: The done thing is about what people are expected to do socially, not about events or feelings.

qs.q: 'Texting at a funeral is a no-no.' Which phrase is NOT close in meaning to 'is a no-no'?
o: is the done thing
is frowned upon
is just not acceptable
is not the done thing
qs.why: A no-no is the opposite of the done thing: it is behaviour people do not accept.

qs.q: Complete the sentence. 'Our new director is lovely: she laughs at her own mistakes because she doesn't ___.'
o: take herself too seriously
think on her feet
get into a whole thing
have a mare
qs.why: To take yourself too seriously is to think you are more important than you are; the opposite fits a person who laughs at herself.

qs.q: Complete the sentence. 'Honestly, it would take an hour to explain, so I'd rather not ___ now.'
o: get into a whole thing
have a no-no
think on the spot
be the done thing
qs.why: Get into a whole thing means to start a long explanation or argument you would rather avoid.

qs.q: Which day would someone jokingly call 'a mare'?
o: The lift broke, my coffee spilled and the train was late.
I lost my job, my home and my savings in one week.
I won a small prize in the office raffle.
I finished my work early and went home.
qs.why: Mare is a mild, humorous word for a day of small annoyances, not for a real disaster.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: First listen once without the text, with three gist questions in mind: What is the difference between exaggeration and understatement? Why do British people like understatement? What can 'It's all good' hide? Then read the transcript, underline the chunks from your list and any new ones, and do not look up every word.

qs.q: Pippa says a friend greets her with just 'Alright?'. What does Pippa conclude?
o: It simply means hello, and the friend does not want to hear about her day
The friend is checking whether she looks ill and wants every detail
The friend is hinting that she has seemed upset for some time
The friend is being ironic about her usual bad mood
qs.why: Pippa says the friend means 'hello' and does not want to hear about her day.

qs.q: Which of these is Pippa's example of understatement?
o: Calling an awful restaurant meal 'less than perfect'
Describing a delayed bus as 'an absolute nightmare'
Saying 'I could eat a horse' when you are hungry
Answering 'Alright?' with a long account of your day
qs.why: Pippa imagines an awful meal described only as 'less than perfect'; the horse example is hyperbole.

qs.q: What does Derek Bousfield suggest about understatement?
o: A mild-sounding remark can signal that something much more serious has happened
It is used to make small problems sound far bigger than they are
Speakers use it when they cannot find stronger words in English
It is mainly a way of flattering people you have just met
qs.why: Derek says understatement signals that something much more serious has gone on.

qs.q: In the imaginary toe-stepping scene, why does Michael Rosen say 'It's all good'?
o: He wants to avoid a long argument with someone he does not know
He thinks it is rude to show pain in front of older people
He wants the stranger to feel guilty without saying anything
He truly feels nothing, so the words are meant literally
qs.why: Michael says he is a bit miffed but a stranger is not worth a barney or a whole thing.

qs.q: As Michael Rosen uses it, what does 'miffed' mean?
o: Mildly irritated by what someone did
Physically hurt by an accident
Embarrassed in front of strangers
Furious and ready to shout
qs.why: Michael explains it himself: 'a little bit annoyed'.

qs.q: In Derek's remark that not taking yourself too seriously 'is really the done thing', what does 'the done thing' mean?
o: The behaviour people expect in that situation
An action that has been finished successfully
A rule written down in company policy
An unusual habit that only a few people have
qs.why: Beth's definition: the behaviour that people consider right in a certain social situation.

qs.q: How does Beth use the word 'hyperbole' at the start?
o: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or humour
Saying less than you feel in order to sound modest
A short, informal form of a longer word
A greeting that needs no real answer
qs.why: Beth introduces hyperbole as exaggeration for emphasis or for humour.

qs.q: In which order does the programme deal with its main topics?
o: Exaggeration, then understatement, then apologising
Understatement, then apologising, then exaggeration
Apologising, then exaggeration, then understatement
Exaggeration, then apologising, then understatement
qs.why: Beth opens with hyperbole, Pippa moves to understatement, and then comes the apology scene.

qs.q: What did the answer to the quiz question reveal about the Greek roots?
o: Huper means 'beyond' and ballo means 'I throw'
Huper means 'beyond' and ballo means 'I speak'
Huper means 'above' and ballo means 'I think'
Huper means 'under' and ballo means 'I throw'
qs.why: Pippa gives the answer a), to overthrow: beyond plus I throw. Beth's guess, over speak, was wrong.

qs.q: What practical advice does Beth give learners at the end?
o: Keep talking to people and treat your own mistakes lightly
Avoid idioms until you fully understand their literal meaning
Check every word in a dictionary before you reply to anyone
Ask native speakers to say exactly what they mean
qs.why: Beth says not to be shy, to get talking, and to say 'No worries!' and carry on after a mistake.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.prompt: Think of a time when someone said 'it's all good' or 'no worries' but you suspected they felt differently. Write 5-7 sentences: what they said, what you think they really felt, why you think so, and what you did. Use at least six phrases from the list and one careful guess about their feelings (for example 'they must have been...' or 'they might have been...').
steps.hint: Good phrases to try: miffed, the done thing, get into a whole thing, a bit of a barney, think on your feet.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Now you will warm up, check which phrases stuck, and listen to a short episode about thinking on your feet. Then comes the main work: the grammar of guessing, predicting and keeping your distance from a claim, which is how fluent speakers sound careful and clever at the same time. You finish with a story told out loud.
steps.ru: Разминка, проверка фраз, короткий выпуск про умение быстро соображать, затем грамматика догадок, прогнозов и осторожных формулировок и рассказ вслух. Это конец первого блока: используйте всё, что уже прошли.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: Listen to the short episode once without the text. Then read the transcript and notice two things: how the presenters explain 'think on your feet' (and what the second expression means), and how they hedge their own words, for example with 'maybe', 'apparently' and 'I'm not sure about'.

steps.title: Guessing, predicting, keeping your distance
steps.text: Deduction has degrees: must (almost certain), is bound to or is likely to (strong prediction), may, might and could (possible), and can't or couldn't (almost certain it is not so), and mustn't is not used for deduction. For the past, put have + participle after the modal: must have been, can't have known; add been + -ing to stress duration, as in must have been waiting. Careful: could have + participle is also used for an unreal past possibility or mild criticism (You could have told me), and should have may mean either regret or expectation (He should have arrived by now). To keep your distance from a claim, use seem or appear with a perfect infinitive (He seems to have left), the pattern It would appear that..., or a reporting passive such as He is said to have resigned.
steps.ru: Степени уверенности: must (почти точно), is bound to / is likely to (сильный прогноз), may, might, could (возможно), can't / couldn't (почти точно нет); mustn't для догадок не используется. Прошлое: модальный + have + V3, а с been + -ing подчёркиваем длительность. Could have и should have могут значить не догадку, а упрёк или ожидание. Дистанция от утверждения: seems / appears to have + V3, It would appear that..., He is said to have...
ex: He said it was all good, but he must have been getting miffed by then.
She can't have meant it literally; she was clearly exaggerating.
Put those two in a small flat for a week and a barney is bound to happen.
You could have told me you were annoyed instead of saying 'no worries'.
It would appear that the complaint was never passed on, which seems to have made things worse.
He is thought to have resigned after the row, though he is unlikely to say so himself.

items.s: Nobody laughed at my joke. They ___ (might / not / get) it, or they were just being polite.
Her eyes are red and swollen. She ___ (must / cry) for a long time.
With the whole family in one small flat for a week, there ___ to be a barney sooner or later.
He hasn't turned up, so he ___ (seem / forget) about the meeting.
It ___ that the message was never sent, though I can't be certain.
To put it mildly, the service was ___ ideal.
You ___ told me you were annoyed instead of saying 'it's all good'.
She's brilliant at thinking on her feet, so she is ___ to be thrown by a surprise question.
Ben left at six and it's only a twenty-minute drive, so he ___ (should / arrive) by now.
She isn't picking up. She ___ (may / drive) right now, so let's try again in ten minutes.
I'm certain he didn't see the sign. -> He ___ the sign.
People say he resigned after the row. -> He ___ after the row.

steps.title: Say it
steps.prompt: Tell a story about a time when you misread someone, or when someone said one thing and you only later understood what they meant. Say what they said, make at least two guesses about what they really thought or felt (must have, might have, can't have), say what you felt sure was going to happen, and add one careful, distancing remark such as 'It would appear that...'. Speak for about a minute and a half.
steps.model: A few weeks ago a client cancelled our meeting at the last minute and just said, "No worries, it's all good." I was a bit miffed, but it's not the done thing to make a fuss, so I had to think quickly on my feet and I suggested a call instead. He must have been under pressure, because he hardly spoke. It would appear that his boss had changed the plan, and he seems to have been embarrassed about it. Afterwards I realised I might have taken it too personally. He was bound to feel awkward, and I could have simply asked him instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Chores and cutting corners
lessons.goal: By the end you can discuss who does what at home and whether it is fair, using phrases like pull your weight, and say how things used to be and how you wish they were.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Today we talk about the least glamorous topic in English: housework, and whether it is ever divided fairly. First you answer a few questions about your own home, then you learn the phrases, then you hear two presenters discuss who does the chores in different parts of the world. These are exactly the words that are easy to miss when you only read books.
steps.ru: Сегодня говорим про быт и справедливость: кто что делает дома. Сначала отвечаешь на вопросы о себе, потом учишь живые фразы, потом слушаешь выпуск и проверяешь, как всё поняла.

steps.title: Warm up
qs: When you were growing up, who made sure the home ran smoothly, and how fairly were the jobs shared between everyone in the family?
Which household job do you put off for as long as you possibly can, and what do you do instead?
Think of a time when somebody did a job for you badly, at home or at work. What happened, and how did you react?
If you could change one thing about the way housework is shared in your home, or in society, what would it be and why?
steps.hint: Write one to three sentences for each question. Say it simply and do not worry about mistakes: you will see better ways of saying it in a minute.

items.ru: делать свою часть работы, не отлынивать
items.ex: In a shared flat, everyone has to pull their weight, even in exam week.
I'll gladly cook every night if you do your fair share of the cleaning up.
We've been at it for hours, so let's take a breather and have some tea.
My teenage son helps out around the house on Sundays, usually after a little persuasion.
Can you take out the bins on your way out? They're overflowing.
We try to split things fifty-fifty, but somehow I always end up doing more.

items.w: take some of the pressure off
items.ex: Buying a dishwasher took some of the pressure off the whole family.
I hate having to nag you about the recycling every single week.
I only deep clean the oven now and then, I'm afraid.

items.ru: когда речь заходит о, что касается
items.ex: When it comes to ironing, I'd honestly rather do it myself.

items.ru: халтурить, делать тяп-ляп, экономить на качестве
items.ex: The builders cut corners, and now the bathroom ceiling leaks.

items.ru: сделать больше, чем от тебя ждут; выложиться
items.ex: Our cleaner really went the extra mile and even sorted out the spice rack.

qs.q: A: Why are you so annoyed with Dan? B: He's out every evening and I'm left with everything. He really needs to ___.
o: pull his weight
take a breather
cut corners
go the extra mile
qs.why: To pull your weight is to work as hard as everyone else, which is exactly what B says Dan does not do.

qs.q: We had been cleaning since eight, so around eleven we took a breather on the balcony. What did we do?
o: We stopped for a short rest
We aired the whole flat
We carried on, but more slowly
We gave up and left the rest
qs.why: To take a breather is to pause briefly and rest.

qs.q: Which sentence uses 'cut corners' correctly?
o: The landlord cut corners on the repairs, so the pipes were leaking within a month.
To make sure everything was perfect, we cut corners and checked every detail twice.
The cleaners cut corners, which is why the flat was spotless and the client delighted.
He never cuts corners, so he usually finishes his jobs in half the time.
qs.why: Cutting corners means doing something the quick or cheap way, so the result is usually poor, as with the leaking pipes.

qs.q: Which expression is NOT close in meaning to 'go the extra mile'?
o: do the bare minimum
go above and beyond
make a special effort
do more than is expected
qs.why: Going the extra mile means doing more than is expected, so doing the bare minimum is the opposite.

qs.q: 'Hiring a cleaner took some of the pressure off us.' What does this mean?
o: Life became less stressful for us
We began to work much faster
The flat looked cleaner than ever
It cost us less than we expected
qs.why: To take pressure off someone is to reduce their stress or workload.

qs.q: 'My mother nags me to ring her every Sunday.' What does she do?
o: She keeps reminding me, which is irritating
She asks me once, very politely
She rings me first so I do not have to
She forgets to ask me at all
qs.why: To nag is to keep asking or complaining in a way that annoys the other person.

qs.q: Which word completes the sentence? 'I don't mind cooking every night, but I'd like you to do your fair ___ of the cleaning.'
o: share
weight
part
turn
qs.why: The fixed phrase is do your fair share; 'weight' belongs to pull your weight, a different phrase.

qs.q: Which option completes the sentence? '___ cooking for a crowd, my gran can beat anyone.'
o: When it comes to
When it goes to
While it comes to
As it comes at
qs.why: When it comes to + noun/-ing introduces the subject you are talking about; the other versions are near-misses that English does not use.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: Press play and listen once with the text closed. Keep three gist questions in mind: whose experience of housework do we hear first, which two places or projects are described, and which chore turns out to be the most hated in Britain? Then read the transcript, underline the chunks you could use at home, and do not look up every word.

qs.q: How does Neil say he and his wife divide the housework?
o: Whoever is not at work at that moment does the jobs
He does the weekends and she does the weekdays
They take turns, one week each, with every chore
She does the cooking and he does the cleaning
qs.why: Neil says that when he is not working he does things, and when his wife is not working she does things.

qs.q: Why did Pippa guess that the oven was the most hated chore?
o: She hates that job herself and hardly ever does it
Her husband had told her it was the worst one
She had read last year's survey results
She had cleaned her own oven that morning
qs.why: Pippa says she chose the oven because she really hates that job and hardly ever does it.

qs.q: What do the UN Women figures suggest?
o: About three more hours a day for women than for men, spent on unpaid care and housework
Women spend about three hours a week more than men on cooking and cleaning
Women do three times as much housework as men in every country
Men and women in wealthy countries spend about the same time on housework
qs.why: Pippa cites UN Women: women around the world do roughly three extra hours of unpaid care and housework daily.

qs.q: According to Neil, what makes household jobs on the island of Rote so time-consuming?
o: Few machines for washing clothes and no water from taps
Most families keep animals that need feeding twice a day
The houses are large and far apart from each other
Women have to finish the fieldwork before they start
qs.why: Neil explains that without many washing machines or running water, chores take a long time.

qs.q: Which order matches the programme?
o: Two listeners describe their homes, the quiz question is set, then Rote, then Croatia
Rote, then two listeners describe their homes, then Croatia, then the quiz question
Croatia, then Rote, then the quiz question, then two listeners describe their homes
The quiz question, then two listeners describe their homes, then Croatia, then Rote
qs.why: The programme opens with the listeners, Neil sets the quiz question, and the Rote project comes before the Croatian one.

qs.q: Anamarija Sočo says mothers get more space for careers, hobbies or 'just to take a breather'. What does 'take a breather' mean here?
o: Pause and rest for a short time
Move out of the city for a while
Start learning a new hobby
Do some breathing exercises
qs.why: Pippa glosses it as a casual way of saying you stop and relax for a bit.

qs.q: Ade Mardiyati says women on Rote 'also help out in the fields'. What is she implying?
o: The claim that the work is split fairly does not hold up, because women carry more
Men on Rote refuse to do any farming or fishing at all
Women choose fieldwork because they dislike housework
The NGO wants women to leave the farming to men
qs.why: She answers the idea of a 'fair division of labour' by pointing out that women do the home tasks and fieldwork too.

qs.q: What does 'women's work' mean as it is used in the programme?
o: A negative label for boring, repetitive jobs usually done by women
Jobs that women happen to do better than men
Paid jobs in which most of the employees are women
Housework that women enjoy more than anything else
qs.why: Neil describes it as a negative expression for dull, repeated tasks that women have traditionally done.

qs.q: When women joke that 'women tend to nag less', what are they suggesting?
o: When men share the work, women have less to complain about
Men have finally started to listen to what women say
Women become too busy to complain about anything
Men do the nagging instead once they take over
qs.why: Anamarija says women joke this when their partners start pulling their weight, so the joke is about having fewer reasons to nag.

qs.q: Ade Mardiyati says you might think 'it's just a fair division of labour'. What idea is behind the phrase 'division of labour'?
o: Different groups do different tasks, so each has its own job
Everyone shares every task exactly equally
Each person does whichever job they most enjoy
Pay is shared out according to how hard a job is
qs.why: Pippa's definition: work is split so that different groups of people handle different tasks.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.prompt: Write 6 to 8 sentences about who does what at home. Say who really pulls their weight and who does not, what you put off for as long as you can, and one thing you would change to make the split fairer. Use at least six phrases from the list and one contrast such as 'although', 'whereas' or 'even though'.
steps.hint: Start with 'When it comes to the housework, ...' and add jobs you know, like unload the dishwasher, mop the floor or do the washing-up.

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Now we revise yesterday's phrases, listen to a short episode about taking shortcuts at work, and go deeper into the grammar of the past: habits, getting used to things, regrets and complaints, and emphatic word order. At the end you tell a short story about your own home, then and now.
steps.ru: Повторяем фразы, слушаем короткий выпуск про халтуру, затем разбираем грамматику уровня C1: used to / would, be и get used to, wish / if only / would rather и инверсию для выразительности. В конце рассказываем про свой дом: как было и как есть.

steps.title: Listen and read
steps.how: Listen to the short episode first without reading and try to picture the athletics track. Then read the transcript and notice how the presenters move from the literal meaning to the metaphorical one, and which two expressions they give for the opposite idea. Afterwards think of one time somebody cut corners for you.

steps.title: Grammar: the past, regrets and emphasis
steps.text: Used to covers past habits and past states, but would is possible only for repeated actions and needs the past time to be clear: 'We used to have a rota, and every Sunday he would swap his turn.' Be used to and get used to take a noun or -ing form because to is a preposition: 'I'm not used to being nagged.' For wishes, use the past simple for the present (I wish we had a dishwasher), the past perfect for regrets (I wish I had asked), and would for annoying behaviour in someone else (I wish he would stop), while would rather needs a past form after a new subject (I'd rather you did it now). To add emphasis, put a negative or restrictive adverbial first and invert the subject and auxiliary: 'Not only does he help, but he never complains.'
steps.ru: Used to — привычки и состояния в прошлом; would — только повторяющиеся действия, когда время понятно. Be/get used to + существительное или -ing (to — предлог). Wish + Past Simple — о настоящем, + Past Perfect — сожаление о прошлом, + would — раздражает чужое поведение; would rather + другое подлежащее + прошедшая форма. Для усиления: отрицательное наречие в начале и инверсия (Not only does he..., Never have I...).
ex: We used to have a rota on the fridge, and every Sunday my brother would try to swap his turn.
It took me years to get used to sharing a kitchen, and I'm still not used to being nagged about the bins.
I wish you would stop leaving wet towels on the bed.
If only we had agreed on a rota from the start, we wouldn't be arguing about it now.
I'd rather you did the washing-up tonight than promised to do it tomorrow.
Not only does he pull his weight, but he never nags anyone about theirs.

items.s: We ___ (not / have) a washing machine in our first flat, so Dad took everything to the launderette.
Every Saturday morning my mum ___ turn the radio up and start scrubbing the kitchen floor.
I ___ hate ironing, but now I find it almost relaxing.
I'm not used to ___ (be) told how to load my own dishwasher.
It took Mia a year to get used to ___ (share) a bathroom with three other people.
I wish we ___ (have) a bigger kitchen; two people can't cook in here at the same time.
I regret leaving the oven until last. -> I wish I ___ (do) it first.
My flatmate leaves his plates in the sink every night. I wish he ___ (stop) doing it.
I'd rather you ___ (not / leave) the washing-up until the morning.
I'd rather you ___ (tell) me yesterday that we had run out of bin bags.
Not only ___ my brother clear up after himself, but he also washes everyone else's mugs.
Honestly, never in my life ___ I seen anyone clean a bathroom so fast.

steps.title: Say it
steps.prompt: Tell the story of how housework was shared in the home you grew up in, and how it works in your life now. Say what people used to do, what you have had to get used to, what you wish were different, and what you would rather change. Use at least three structures from the grammar and two phrases from the lessons.
steps.model: When I was a child, my mum used to do almost everything at home, and every evening she would collapse on the sofa, exhausted. My dad meant well, but he never really pulled his weight. Now I live with my partner, and I've had to get used to sharing a small kitchen. Not only does he do his fair share, he never complains about it. Still, I wish he would stop leaving the cupboard doors open! If only my dad had helped out more back then, my mum could have taken a proper breather. I'd rather we split everything evenly than keep score.

lessons.title: Retail therapy and clever ads
lessons.goal: By the end you can tell a natural story about a purchase you made on impulse or under someone's influence, using passive and causative structures and the phrases from the lesson.

sources.title: How advertisers make us spend money

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Why did you buy the last thing you bought? Today you will listen to two BBC presenters talk about how adverts, shop assistants and even screens quietly push us to spend. You will collect phrases you can use tomorrow when you talk about your own shopping and your moods.
steps.ru: Сегодня разберём, как реклама и магазины незаметно подталкивают нас к покупкам, и соберём живые фразы, чтобы рассказывать о своём шопинге и настроении.

steps.title: Warm up
qs: Think of the last time you bought something you did not really need. What made you do it, and how did you feel an hour later?
When you are not sure what to choose, whose advice or example do you tend to follow, and why them rather than someone else?
Have you ever said yes to something extra in a shop or a café just to avoid an awkward moment? Or have you ever talked your way out of something and got away with it?
Imagine you have almost no money but you still want to organise a lovely surprise for a friend. How would you solve the problem?
steps.hint: Answer in two or three sentences each and say what you really think, not what sounds clever.

steps.title: Grammar: passive and causatives at C1
steps.text: At C1 the passive is a choice of style. Modals and perfect forms are common: 'It should have been checked' and 'This offer may be withdrawn'. Reporting verbs give the impersonal passive, 'It is said that...' or 'He is believed to have...' (earlier time) and 'is thought to be -ing' (happening now). Advertisers and formal writers like it because the speaker disappears: 'Customers are advised...', 'It has been proved...'. For causatives, 'have/get something done' covers services and bad luck, 'get somebody to do' means persuade, and 'make' takes a bare infinitive in the active but 'to' in the passive: 'We were made to wait'.
steps.ru: Пассив на уровне C1: с модальными и перфектными формами (should have been checked, may be withdrawn); безличный пассив с глаголами речи и мнения (It is said that, He is believed to have...: to have + 3-я форма для более раннего действия, to be + -ing для происходящего сейчас); так пишут в рекламе и официально (Customers are advised...). Каузатив: have/get something done (услуга или неприятность), get somebody to do (уговорить), make: в активе без to, в пассиве с to (We were made to wait).

sources.title: Comparisons as Predictable as the Sunrise
Like a moth to a flame

steps.title: Today
steps.text: Native speakers love comparisons: someone is as cool as a cucumber, an explanation is as clear as mud, a grandfather is as fit as a fiddle. Today you will warm up with some questions about yourself, meet twelve spoken phrases, and then read a data story about which comparisons writers really use and why some of them last while others fade.
steps.ru: Носители языка постоянно сравнивают: «спокойный как огурец», «ясно как грязь», «здоров как скрипка». Сегодня ответишь на вопросы о себе, выучишь 12 фраз и прочитаешь статью с данными о том, какие сравнения на самом деле используют авторы и почему одни живут, а другие уходят.

Do people around you use a lot of ready-made comparisons when they talk, like 'strong as a bull'? Which ones do you still hear, and which sound old-fashioned to you now?

steps.title: Read the story
steps.how: First skim once for gist with three questions in mind: What kind of similes does the author study, and where from? What is the difference between a 'specialist' and a 'generalist' noun? What is special about 'as clear as mud'? Then read it again more slowly. Do not look up every word.

qs.q: Which pair of comparisons does the author give as having survived, and which as having faded?
o: Survived: 'busy as a bee', 'fit as a fiddle'. Faded: 'drunk as a lord', 'rich as Croesus'.
Survived: 'drunk as a lord', 'rich as Croesus'. Faded: 'busy as a bee', 'fit as a fiddle'.
Survived: 'busy as a bee', 'rich as Croesus'. Faded: 'fit as a fiddle', 'drunk as a lord'.
Survived: 'fit as a fiddle', 'drunk as a lord'. Faded: 'busy as a bee', 'rich as Croesus'.
qs.why: The author says 'as busy as a bee' and 'as fit as a fiddle' have endured, while 'as drunk as a lord' and 'as rich as Croesus' have fallen out of fashion.

qs.q: Why did the author choose the 'as ___ as ___' form to study?
o: Its fixed structure makes it easy to find automatically with little human judgement.
It is the only form of simile that appears in popular fiction at all.
It gives the most vivid pictures, which suits a story for readers.
It is the form that readers find easiest to remember and repeat.
qs.why: The author explains that other figurative forms are hard to extract at scale, while this one has a rigid structure.

qs.q: What does the author say about the adjective 'dry'?
o: Bone, desert and dust together cover 43% of uses, then usage falls away quickly.
Bone alone covers 43% of uses, and no other noun comes close to it.
Its three top nouns are used about equally, with no clear drop after them.
It has a gentle slope, so no single idiom dominates the comparisons.
qs.why: For 'dry' the top three nouns make up 43%, followed by a quick drop-off and a long tail of rarer choices.

qs.q: What does the 92% figure in the story tell us?
o: Two random 'as ___ as a cucumber' similes would almost certainly both be about 'cool'.
92% of all similes about being cool in the data use the noun 'cucumber'.
Cucumber appears in 92% of the similes that the author collected.
Hell is paired with 92% of the 500 adjectives in the analysis.
qs.why: The 92% is the chance that two randomly chosen cucumber similes share the adjective 'cool', which is why cucumber is the model specialist.

qs.q: As the author uses the terms, what makes a noun a 'generalist'?
o: It appears in similes with many different adjectives.
It is used by a large number of different authors.
It has several different literal meanings in English.
It is found more often in older novels than new ones.
qs.why: Generalists serve in similes for dozens of adjectives, while specialists belong to just one quality.

qs.q: In 'sexy as hell', what does the author mean by saying 'hell' works as an 'amplifier'?
o: It simply makes the quality stronger, like 'very', without painting a picture.
It adds a religious image of danger to the quality being described.
It shows that the speaker is joking about the quality.
It tells us that the quality is a negative one.
qs.why: The author says similes usually work because the noun has the quality, but hell often just means 'very', as in 'cute as hell'.

qs.q: What does the story say about 'cat' in similes?
o: Writers use it for a wide range of qualities, and it is the top noun for four adjectives.
It is tied almost entirely to one adjective, in the way cucumber is tied to cool.
It mostly stands for defencelessness and innocence in the fiction studied.
It is mainly a stand-in for 'nothing is happening here' in similes.
qs.why: The author says cat spans everything from graceful to weak and is the most used noun for nervous, active, agile and nimble.

qs.q: Why, in the author's view, do ironic similes tend to work best with positive adjectives?
o: The positive word sets up an expectation and the noun delivers the punchline.
Positive adjectives are rare, so the comparison attracts more attention.
Negative adjectives already sound ironic, so the noun adds nothing.
Writers in older books used positive adjectives for jokes more often.
qs.why: The author says ironic similes work best with positive-sentiment adjectives 'setting up the noun as the punch line'.

qs.q: 'Most animals are pigeon-holed': what does 'pigeon-holed' suggest here?
o: Each animal is stuck with one typical quality in similes.
Animals are kept apart from human characters in novels.
Writers avoid using animals in comparisons.
Animals are mostly compared to birds.
qs.why: The author contrasts animals such as the mule (stubborn) with the cat, which covers a huge range of behaviour.

qs.q: What does the author admit about the dataset?
o: It is reliable for overall patterns, but single sentences may be wrongly classified.
Careful filtering means that no false matches remain in the final data.
The overall patterns are unreliable, but individual sentences are accurate.
It is reliable only for the hundred most common adjectives in English.
qs.why: The author says the data is accurate overall but imperfect for individual sentences; false positives were filtered out, but not completely removed.

steps.title: Today

steps.title: Comparing things at C1 level
steps.text: For proportion, repeat the + comparative: the longer I wait, the less I want it. Multiples go before as ... as (twice as, three times as, half as), and 'not nearly as' or 'nowhere near as' says the gap is big. Never put 'very' before a comparative; use far, much or considerably, and use 'by far' or 'easily' with a superlative. 'Like' takes a noun, but 'as if' and 'as though' take a clause, and for an unreal idea the verb goes back a step: she talks as if she owned the place. After than and as you can leave words out: it cost more than we had budgeted (for).
steps.ru: Пропорция: the + сравнительная ... the + сравнительная. Кратность ставится перед as ... as (twice as, half as), а not nearly as / nowhere near as показывает большую разницу. Перед сравнительной степенью нельзя very: нужны far, much, considerably; с превосходной степенью by far. After like идёт существительное, after as if / as though идёт целое предложение, и для нереального глагол сдвигается в прошедшее. После than и as часть слов можно опустить.

Spending is considerably higher in December than in any other month, and it is by far the most tempting time of year.
She spends as if there were no tomorrow, but she is not nearly as relaxed as she looks.
He talks about his savings as though he owned half the street.
The bill came to a good deal more than we had budgeted for, so it was not so much a treat as a mistake.

steps.title: Say it
steps.prompt: Tell a short story about a time you spent money you had not planned to spend, or give your opinion on how people deal with money and stress. Use at least three structures from the lesson (the more..., the less...; a multiple or 'nowhere near as ... as'; 'by far' or 'considerably' with a comparison; 'as if') and two or more of the phrases.
targets: like a moth to a flame
steps.model: When it comes to money, I'm nowhere near as sensible as I would like to be. Online sales pull me in like a moth to a flame, and the more I scroll, the more I spend. Last month I bought a lamp I did not need, and my mum reacted as if I had bought a car. Normally she is as cool as a cucumber, so that was a surprise. Still, by far the most useful thing I own is a spreadsheet she made for me, so now I check it before I click. I'm slowly getting better, and my mood is considerably calmer than it was in the spring.
